lessons.title: Common Verbs: Daily Actions
lessons.body: In Swahili, everyday actions are expressed with verbs that you will use constantly. Start with these ten: kula (to eat), kunywa (to drink), kulala (to sleep), kuamka (to wake up), kwenda (to go), kuja (to come), kufanya kazi (to work), kusoma (to read/study), kuandika (to write), and kupika (to cook). Notice that all infinitives begin with 'ku-'. To make a simple command or a present tense statement, you remove 'ku-' and add the correct subject prefix. For example, 'Ninakula' means 'I eat' or 'I am eating'. The prefix 'ni-' means 'I'. For 'you' (singular), use 'u-': 'Unakula' = you eat. For 'he/she', use 'a-': 'Anakula' = he/she eats. For 'we', use 'tu-': 'Tunakula' = we eat. For 'you' (plural), use 'm-': 'Mnakula' = you all eat. For 'they', use 'wa-': 'Wanakula' = they eat. Practice these with each verb. In daily life, you might say 'Ninaamka saa mbili asubuhi' (I wake up at 8 AM) â note that Swahili time starts at 6 AM, so 'saa mbili' is 8 AM. 'Ninakunywa chai' (I drink tea). 'Ninakwenda sokoni' (I go to the market). 'Ninapika ugali' (I cook ugali). These verbs are the backbone of describing your day. To make the negative, change the prefix: 'si-' for I, 'hu-' for you, 'ha-' for he/she, 'hatu-' for we, 'ham-' for you all, 'hawa-' for they. So 'Sili' = I don't eat. 'Hakunywi' = he doesn't drink. Practice by narrating your morning: 'Naamka, ninasali, ninakunywa chai, ninakwenda kazini.' With these ten verbs, you can already describe most of your daily routine. Write them on flashcards and review them as you go about your day.

lessons.title: Present Tense Verb Conjugation
lessons.body: Swahili present tense is formed by combining a subject prefix, the tense marker '-na-', and the verb stem. The formula is: Subject Prefix + 'na' + Verb Stem. For example, 'kupika' (to cook) becomes 'ninapika' (I cook), 'unapika' (you cook), 'anapika' (he/she cooks), 'tunapika' (we cook), 'mnapika' (you all cook), 'wanapika' (they cook). The subject prefixes are: ni- (I), u- (you singular), a- (he/she), tu- (we), m- (you plural), wa- (they). Note that for 'I' and 'we', the prefix is 'ni-' and 'tu-', but before vowels they may change slightly; however, with '-na-' they remain consistent. For negative present, replace '-na-' with '-i-' and change the subject prefix for some persons: si- (I), hu- (you), ha- (he/she), hatu- (we), ham- (you all), hawa- (they). So 'sipiki' (I don't cook), 'hupiki' (you don't cook), 'hapiki' (he/she doesn't cook), 'hatupiki' (we don't cook), 'hampiki' (you all don't cook), 'hawapiki' (they don't cook). The verb stem may change slightly in the negative; for example, 'kula' becomes 'li' in 'sili' (I don't eat). Practice with common verbs: 'kusoma' (to read) -> 'ninasoma' (I read), 'kusikiliza' (to listen) -> 'unasikiliza' (you listen), 'kuandika' (to write) -> 'anaandika' (he writes). To ask questions, simply use the same form with a rising intonation: 'Unasoma?' (Are you reading?). To answer yes, say 'Ndiyo, ninasoma.' No: 'Hapana, sisomi.' Use these patterns to talk about what you do regularly. For example, 'Kila siku, ninaamka saa mbili, ninasali, na ninakunywa chai.' (Every day, I wake up at 8, pray, and drink tea.) With practice, conjugation becomes automatic.

lessons.title: Talking About Your Daily Routine
lessons.body: Describing your daily routine in Swahili helps you communicate with others about your life. Start with the time you wake up: 'Ninaamka saa ngapi?' (What time do you wake up?) Answer: 'Ninaamka saa mbili asubuhi' (I wake up at 8 AM). Remember Swahili time: saa moja = 7 AM, saa mbili = 8 AM, etc. Then say what you do next: 'Ninasali' (I pray), 'Ninapiga mswaki' (I brush my teeth), 'Ninaoga' (I bathe), 'Ninakunywa chai' (I drink tea), 'Ninakula kifungua kinywa' (I eat breakfast). For breakfast, common foods are 'mkate' (bread), 'chai' (tea), 'mayai' (eggs). Then you might go to work: 'Ninaenda kazini' (I go to work). If you are a farmer, 'Ninaenda shambani' (I go to the farm). If you are a student, 'Ninaenda shule' (I go to school). At midday, 'Ninakula chakula cha mchana' (I eat lunch). In the afternoon, 'Ninafanya kazi' (I work) or 'Ninasoma' (I study). In the evening, 'Ninarudi nyumbani' (I return home), 'Ninapika' (I cook), 'Ninakula chakula cha jioni' (I eat dinner). Before bed, 'Ninaangalia televisheni' (I watch TV), 'Ninasoma kitabu' (I read a book), 'Ninalala' (I sleep). To connect actions, use 'kisha' (then) or 'baada ya' (after). For example: 'Ninaamka saa mbili, kisha ninaoga, na baada ya hapo ninakunywa chai.' (I wake up at 8, then I bathe, and after that I drink tea.) Practice by writing your own routine from morning to night. Use specific times and activities. Share it with a partner and ask each other questions. This builds fluency and vocabulary.

lessons.title: Adverbs of Frequency
lessons.body: Adverbs of frequency tell how often you do something. In Swahili, common ones are: 'kila siku' (every day), 'kila mara' (always), 'mara nyingi' (often), 'wakati mwingine' (sometimes), 'mara chache' (rarely), 'kamwe' (never). These usually come after the verb or at the beginning of the sentence. For example: 'Ninakunywa chai kila siku' (I drink tea every day). 'Mara nyingi, ninasoma vitabu' (Often, I read books). 'Wakati mwingine, ninachelewa' (Sometimes, I am late). 'Mara chache, ninakula nyama' (Rarely, I eat meat). 'Kamwe, ninakunywa pombe' (I never drink alcohol). Note: 'kamwe' is often used with negative verbs: 'Sikunywi pombe kamwe' (I never drink alcohol). To ask 'how often?', say 'Mara ngapi?' For example: 'Unakunywa chai mara ngapi?' (How often do you drink tea?) Answer: 'Mara moja kwa siku' (Once a day) or 'Mara mbili kwa siku' (Twice a day). You can also use 'kila' with time expressions: 'kila asubuhi' (every morning), 'kila jioni' (every evening), 'kila wiki' (every week), 'kila mwezi' (every month). Practice by placing these adverbs in sentences about your routine. For example: 'Kila asubuhi, ninaamka saa mbili. Mara nyingi, ninakunywa chai. Wakati mwingine, ninachelewa kufika kazini. Kamwe, sipendi kuchelewa.' (Every morning, I wake up at 8. Often, I drink tea. Sometimes, I am late to work. I never like to be late.) This helps you express habits and frequency accurately.

lessons.title: Hobbies and Leisure Activities
lessons.body: Talking about hobbies and leisure in Swahili allows you to connect with others and share your interests. Common hobbies include: 'kusoma vitabu' (reading books), 'kucheza mpira' (playing football), 'kuimba' (singing), 'kucheza ngoma' (dancing), 'kupiga picha' (taking photos), 'kupenda muziki' (listening to music), 'kupanda baiskeli' (riding a bicycle), 'kuogelea' (swimming), 'kupika' (cooking), 'kulima' (farming). To say 'I like to...', use 'Ninapenda' + infinitive: 'Ninapenda kusoma vitabu' (I like to read books). To say 'I don't like', use 'Sipendi' + infinitive: 'Sipendi kucheza mpira' (I don't like to play football). To ask someone about their hobbies: 'Unapenda kufanya nini wakati wa mapumziko?' (What do you like to do during leisure time?) Answer: 'Ninapenda kucheza ngoma na kuimba' (I like to dance and sing). You can also ask 'Una hobby gani?' (What hobby do you have?) Note that 'hobby' is borrowed from English. In African contexts, leisure activities often include communal events: 'kushiriki harusi' (attending weddings), 'kushiriki sherehe' (attending celebrations), 'kucheza bao' (playing bao, a traditional board game). For example: 'Wakati wa mapumziko, ninapenda kucheza bao na marafiki zangu.' (During leisure time, I like to play bao with my friends.) To express frequency, combine with adverbs: 'Mara nyingi, ninapenda kutembea pwani' (Often, I like to walk on the beach). Practice by listing your hobbies and asking others. This vocabulary enriches your conversations and helps you make plans.

lessons.title: Making Plans with Friends
lessons.body: Making plans with friends in Swahili involves suggesting activities, agreeing, and setting times. Start with a suggestion: 'Twende...' (Let's go...). For example: 'Twende sokoni' (Let's go to the market), 'Twende kwenye mgahawa' (Let's go to the restaurant), 'Twende kuogelea' (Let's go swimming). To ask 'Do you want to...?', say 'Unataka...?' + infinitive: 'Unataka kwenda sinema?' (Do you want to go to the cinema?) To agree, say 'Ndiyo, twende!' (Yes, let's go!) or 'Sawa, niko tayari' (Okay, I'm ready). To disagree, say 'Samahani, siwezi' (Sorry, I can't) or 'Sina muda' (I don't have time). To suggest a time: 'Tukutane saa ngapi?' (What time shall we meet?) Answer: 'Tukutane saa nne' (Let's meet at 10 AM â remember saa nne = 10 AM). Or 'Tukutane jioni' (Let's meet in the evening). To confirm: 'Tutaonana kesho' (See you tomorrow). 'Tutaonana baadaye' (See you later). For making plans by phone: 'Unapiga simu?' (Are you calling?) 'Ninafurahi kukusikia' (I'm happy to hear you). Then discuss: 'Leo jioni, una shughuli?' (This evening, do you have plans?) If not: 'Twende kwenye sherehe' (Let's go to a party). If yes: 'Tutaonana kesho' (See you tomorrow). Practice with a friend: one suggests, the other responds. Use real scenarios like going to a football match, a wedding, or a market. This builds confidence in social interactions.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Daily Activities and Routines in Swahili for African Agribusiness

This Practical Reference lesson consolidates the six lessons in the Daily Activities and Routines module. It is written for African agribusiness professionals â traders, cooperative managers, extension officers, logistics coordinators, and cross-border entrepreneurs â who need to speak about work schedules, market days, farm routines, deliveries, and leisure with clarity and confidence in Swahili. Swahili is the most widely spoken lingua franca in East Africa, with an estimated 200 million speakers across Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda, the DRC, Rwanda, Burundi, Mozambique, and beyond. For agribusiness, it is a working language of trade: from the produce markets of Dar es Salaam and Nairobi to the coffee cooperatives of Mbeya and the fisheries of Mwanza. Mastering daily-routine language lets you negotiate schedules, confirm delivery times, discuss planting and harvest cycles, and build the personal rapport that underpins trust-based trade.

Use this reference as a desk tool. It gathers the core verbs, tense patterns, frequency adverbs, hobby vocabulary, and planning phrases into one place, with tables you can print and a checklist you can apply before any meeting, market visit, or field day.

1. Core Verbs for Daily Agribusiness Actions

These verbs recur constantly in trade and farm routines. Learn them with their infinitive (ku-) form and their present-tense first-person form (ni-), which you will use most when describing your own day.

Table 1: Essential daily-action verbs for agribusiness
Swahili (infinitive) Present (I ...) English Business use
kuamkaninaamkato wake upDescribe start of day before market
kwendanaendato goGoing to farm, market, warehouse
kufikanafikato arriveConfirm delivery arrival time
kupimanapimato measure/weighWeighing produce, grading
kuuzanauzato sellSales transactions
kununuananunuato buyProcurement from farmers
kulipanalipato payPayments to suppliers
kupanganapangato plan/arrangePlanning schedules and prices
kukutananakutanato meetMeeting buyers, cooperatives
kufunganafungato closeClosing shop or deal
kupumzikanapumzikato restEnd-of-day routine
kulalanalalato sleepClosing the day

Source: Verb inventory compiled from Kamusi ya Kiswahili Sanifu (TUKI, University of Dar es Salaam) and the Peace Corps Tanzania Kiswahili Language Manual (public domain training material).

2. Present Tense Conjugation Pattern

Swahili present tense is built with a subject prefix + tense marker -na- + verb root. For "I" the prefix is ni-, giving ni-na- + root. This single pattern covers most daily-routine statements.

Table 2: Present-tense subject prefixes with the verb kufanya (to do)
Subject Prefix + -na- Full form English
Mimi (I)ni-na-ninafanyaI do / I am doing
Wewe (you sg.)u-na-unafanyaYou do
Yeye (he/she)a-na-anafanyaHe/she does
Sisi (we)tu-na-tunafanyaWe do
Ninyi (you pl.)m-na-munafanyaYou (all) do
Wao (they)wa-na-wanafanyaThey do

Source: Conjugation paradigm based on Swahili Grammar for Introductory and Intermediate Levels (University Press of America) and the University of Florida Swahili Language Handbook (open-access).

3. Frequency Adverbs and Time Markers

Frequency adverbs let you describe how often a routine happens â vital for planning supply cycles and confirming reliability with partners.

  • kila siku â every day
  • mara nyingi â often
  • kila mara â always
  • mara chache â rarely
  • kamwe / sijawahi â never
  • wakati mwingine â sometimes
  • asubuhi â morning; mchana â afternoon; jioni â evening; usiku â night
  • leo â today; kesho â tomorrow; jana â yesterday

Example: Mara nyingi naenda sokoni asubuhi, lakini wakati mwingine nafika mchana. â "I often go to the market in the morning, but sometimes I arrive in the afternoon."

4. Hobbies, Leisure, and Relationship Building

In African agribusiness, deals are built on relationships. Being able to talk about leisure â football, music, family, church or mosque activities, farming as a hobby â turns a transaction into a partnership. Useful phrases:

  • Napenda kucheza mpira. â I like playing football.
  • Napenda kusikiliza muziki. â I like listening to music.
  • Napenda kusafiri. â I like travelling.
  • Wakati wa mapumziko, nalima bustani yangu. â During my free time, I tend my garden.
  • Je, unapenda nini? â What do you like?

5. Making Plans with Friends and Partners

Use these structures to propose meetings, deliveries, or social plans:

  • Tuonane kesho saa tatu. â Let's meet tomorrow at 9 a.m.
  • Unaweza kufika saa ngapi? â What time can you arrive?
  • Nitakuja kesho asubuhi. â I will come tomorrow morning.
  • Tunaweza kupanga mkutano wiki ijayo? â Can we arrange a meeting next week?
  • Samahani, siwezi leo. Kesho vipi? â Sorry, I can't today. How about tomorrow?

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â Time and Money Clarity

Swahili time is counted from dawn (6 a.m. clock = saa kumi na mbili asubuhi). Misreading "saa mbili" as 2 p.m. instead of 8 a.m. has caused missed deliveries and spoiled perishable goods across East African markets. Always confirm the clock time explicitly â say "saa mbili asubuhi, yaani 8:00" â before agreeing to any pickup, payment, or cold-chain delivery. For cash transactions, never confirm amounts by voice alone; write the figure and read it back in Swahili (shilingi elfu hamsini = 50,000 shillings) to prevent costly errors.

6. Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Greet before business. Always open with Habari za asubuhi? (Good morning?) or Shikamoo to elders â rapport precedes negotiation.
  2. State your routine in present tense. Use ni-na- + verb: ninaamka, naenda, nauza, nalipa.
  3. Confirm time in both systems. Say the Swahili hour and the clock time to avoid the 6-hour offset trap.
  4. Use frequency adverbs for reliability. Kila siku (every day) signals dependable supply; mara chache (rarely) warns of scarcity.
  5. Talk hobbies to build trust. Ask Unapenda nini? and share your own leisure interests.
  6. Plan with tuonane and tunaweza. These invite collaboration rather than issuing demands.
  7. Write numbers, then read them back. Prevent payment disputes by confirming amounts in Swahili and on paper.
  8. Close politely. End with Asante sana, tutaonana kesho (Thank you, see you tomorrow).

Further Reading

  • TUKI â Taasisi ya Uchunguzi wa Kiswahili, University of Dar es Salaam â authoritative Swahili dictionaries and grammar references.
  • Peace Corps Tanzania â Kiswahili Language Manual â free downloadable training materials used by volunteers and traders.
  • Kilakwetu Initiative â Swahili for business and trade training resources for East African entrepreneurs.
  • East African Community (EAC) â Language and Culture Portal â regional policy on Swahili as an official working language.
  • Baraza la Kiswahili la Taifa (BAKITA) â Tanzania's national Swahili council, with terminology and standards.

This Practical Reference supports the rise AFRICA Skills course Swahili Language â Daily Activities and Routines. Apply it in real trade settings: at the market, in the cooperative office, on the farm, and in cross-border negotiations. Language is a business asset â use it daily.

quiz.q: What is the Swahili verb for 'to eat'?
Which prefix means 'I' in present tense?
How do you say 'They eat'?
What is the negative form of 'Ninakula' (I eat)?
quiz.explanation: The negative for 'I' is 'si-' and 'kula' becomes 'li', so 'Sili'.

quiz.q: Which verb means 'to cook'?
What is the correct present tense form for 'We drink'?
How do you say 'She doesn't read'?
quiz.explanation: For 'he/she', the negative prefix is 'ha-' and the verb stem changes to 'somi'.

quiz.q: What does 'Ninaamka saa mbili asubuhi' mean?
options: A) I wake up at 6 AM
B) I wake up at 7 AM
C) I wake up at 8 AM
D) I wake up at 9 AM
quiz.explanation: In Swahili time, 'saa mbili' is 8 AM.

quiz.q: Which word means 'then' in a sequence?
How do you say 'I bathe'?
What is the Swahili word for 'breakfast'?
How do you ask 'What time do you wake up?'
quiz.explanation: 'Unaamka saa ngapi?' means 'What time do you wake up?'

quiz.q: What does 'kila siku' mean?
Which adverb means 'often'?
How do you say 'I never drink alcohol'?
quiz.explanation: 'Sikunywi pombe kamwe' uses negative 'si-' and 'kamwe' for 'never'.

quiz.q: What is the question for 'How often?'
Which phrase means 'every morning'?
How do you say 'I like to read books'?
quiz.explanation: 'Ninapenda kusoma vitabu' means 'I like to read books'.

quiz.q: What is 'kucheza mpira'?
Which activity is traditional in East Africa?
quiz.explanation: 'Kucheza bao' is a traditional board game.

quiz.q: How do you ask 'What do you like to do in your free time?'
options: A) Unapenda kufanya nini wakati wa mapumziko?
quiz.explanation: This question asks about leisure activities.

quiz.q: What does 'Twende' mean?
How do you suggest going to the market?
quiz.explanation: 'Twende sokoni' means 'Let's go to the market'.

quiz.q: What is the response 'Sawa, niko tayari'?
How do you ask 'What time shall we meet?'
quiz.explanation: 'Tukutane saa ngapi?' means 'What time shall we meet?'

quiz.q: What does 'Tutaonana kesho' mean?
How do you say 'I'm happy to hear you' on the phone?
quiz.explanation: 'Ninafurahi kukusikia' means 'I'm happy to hear you'.

quiz.q: What is the negative form of 'Ninapenda'?
Which verb means 'to swim'?
What does 'Mara moja kwa siku' mean?
quiz.explanation: 'Mara moja kwa siku' means 'once a day'.
